title: A Trilemma, Not a Verdict
paragraphs: The simulation argument is often summarised as the claim that we are probably living inside a computer. That summary gets its author wrong. In a paper published in two thousand three, the philosopher Nick Bostrom argued for something more cautious: that at least one of three propositions is true.

Either almost every civilisation at our stage dies out before it becomes technologically mature; or mature civilisations are extremely unlikely to run large numbers of simulations of their ancestors; or we are almost certainly simulated ourselves. The reasoning behind the third option is statistical rather than mystical. If simulated minds vastly outnumbered biological ones, then a mind with no way of telling the difference should, on ordinary principles of probability, expect to be among the majority.

Critics have pressed on several joints of this structure. Some doubt that consciousness could arise from computation at all, an assumption the argument needs but does not establish. Others question the indifference principle that licenses the final step, asking why a mind should treat itself as a random sample from all observers rather than from those with experiences like its own. These objections do not refute the argument outright; they relocate the debate to premises that are themselves deeply contested.

The argument also has an older relative. Descartes imagined a deceiving demon capable of feeding him a false world, and used the possibility to ask what, if anything, could be known with certainty. Bostrom's version differs in an instructive way: it does not ask whether we can rule out deception, but how likely deception is, given assumptions about future technology. It trades the absolute doubt of the seventeenth century for a probabilistic doubt suited to an age of computers.

Whether that trade is progress depends on what one wants from philosophy. As a forecast, the argument is no stronger than its premises. As a discipline for reasoning, however, it has real value, because it forces anyone who dismisses it to say exactly which premise they reject, and why.
